newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli army faces tough budget battle.
newsitem.headline: Israeli army faces tough budget battle.

text.p: Israel's army faces a tough battle for more defence spending with Treasury officials asking the government on Sunday to make deep cuts in next year's overall budget.

Defence Minstry director-general Ilan Biran said his office had requested a 1.5 billion shekel rise in military spending and wanted the government to draw up a multi-year plan that would put the defence budget on an upward trajectory.
"Our request was for a supplement of 1.5 billion shekels," said Biran.
He spoke to Reuters hours after Treasury officials asked the government to approve a 2.5 billion shekel cut in the 1998 budget in order to meet its 2.4 percent deficit target.

Biran said years of erosion in defence spending, which stood this year at 30 billion shekels, had created "an acute need for modernising weapons systems and (increasing) preparedness that must be built into a multi-year plan."
Other defence officials, including army chief Amnon Shahak, have warned that readiness for a possible war with Syria had become "intolerable" due to budget constraints.
Israeli intelligence officials have said the risk of war with Syria, a partner in peace talks until they were suspended last year, is higher than in recent years.
Israel has fought several wars with its neighbours and keeps thousands of troops in the West Bank, Gaza Strip and south Lebanon.
Biran said the military had to either refurbish or replace tanks, warplanes and other weapons purchased in the 1970s.
He denied reports the army was spending more than half its budget on salaries and retirement plans for servicemen, putting the figure at less than 33 percent.
Last month the government slashed 206 billion shekels from the 1997 defence budget as part of an overall cut of 800 million shekels.
"We need to cut the total budget by about 2.5 billion shekels in order to maintain the deficit target of 8.5 billion shekels," said Finance Ministry spokesman Motti Sherf.
"Where to cut is the government's decision according to its own priorities. We don't decide where to cut, the government does," Sherf told Reuters.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has faced stiff opposition in previous cuts by nearly every cabinet minister.

Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai boycotted a cabinet meeting last month to protest at the 206 million shekel cut, complaining Treasury officials had gone over his head to deal directly with the prime minister.

Netanyahu, elected 14 months ago on a pledge to beef up security, promised last November to raise defence spending. Officials in his office say lower-than-expected tax revenues made the increase impossible.

The Treasury has set a 1998 budget of 164.4 billion shekels from which it proposes to cut about 2.5 billion shekels. The cabinet will meet on August 31 to vote on the budget before sending it to parliament for approval by year end.
